implementation_notes: JavaScript has no per-instance slot for behaviour: methods written in a class body live once on the prototype and are shared by all instances, so a stateless 'base class' contributes nothing to instance size and the classic empty-base structure collapses into plain prototype inheritance. Multiple stateless behaviours are mixed in by copying methods onto the prototype (Object.assign(MyClass.prototype, mixin)), which allocates nothing per instance; interfaces and type aliases in TypeScript-style toolchains are the same idea with static checking added. Instance size is exactly the set of own properties, so the real levers are constructor assignments, class fields and per-instance closures, which should be kept to the state that actually varies.
pitfalls: this.stamp = () => ... or bound methods in the constructor create one closure per instance, defeating prototype sharing and inflating every object.
Applying a mixin to individual objects instead of the prototype multiplies hidden classes (object shapes) and slows property access across the program.

Private #fields add per-instance slots; private methods are shared through the class's private method machinery rather than becoming per-instance closures, but both remain class-specific and are not interchangeable with public prototype mixins.
